conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers adjust emotionally after birth. I’d like to spend a few minutes with you today using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a short, 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting the right kind of support. Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. If at any point you’d like to pause or talk more about a feeling, we can do that.

We’ll go through each question one by one; I’ll ask it conversationally, and you can answer in your own words. When you’re ready, let’s begin:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly… I can laugh sometimes, maybe if my husband pulls a silly face or the baby does something cute, but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time I don’t really feel amused, even when I know something’s supposed to be funny. It’s like the joy is muffled.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess I’d put myself in the middle—not “yes, most of the time,” but not “definitely not” either. Sometimes a laugh slips out, but it’s pretty rare. I’d say “yes, only occasionally.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more chore. I still do them because I know I should, but that “looking-forward” feeling barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right or my milk isn’t good enough. I’ll replay every little thing I did and wonder what I messed up. Rationally I know some stuff just happens, but the guilt still jumps in first.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet or his color looks “off,” even when he’s fine. Or I’ll lie down and my mind spins about SIDS, choking, the house burning—anything. There’s no real trigger; it just shows up and I can’t shake it for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, that happens too. Sometimes out of nowhere I get this wave of dread—like something awful is about to happen, but I can’t name what. My chest feels tight and I have to remind myself to breathe. It passes after a bit, but it’s scary while it lasts.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. Between the feedings, laundry, and trying to grab a shower, it piles up fast. I’ll sit on the couch at night and think, “I accomplished almost nothing,” even though I’ve been running all day. Sometimes I just stare at the mess and feel frozen.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Lately, yes. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, and then my head starts spinning with everything I think I did wrong or might forget tomorrow. I’ll lie there for an hour or two, sometimes drift off and wake right back up. I’m exhausted, but sleep just won’t come.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, honestly. I wake up and there’s this heavy feeling in my chest before the day even starts. Little things feel like big deals, and I catch myself tearing up for no clear reason. People keep saying I should be happy, but the sadness just hangs around.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it probably happens three or four nights a week. Once the house is quiet, everything I’ve been pushing down all day just hits. I’ll cry in the shower or while I’m pumping—somewhere no one can see. It’s not one big thing; it’s this steady ache that overflows.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I feel low, but I wouldn’t go there. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

You've shared that the sparkle of new motherhood feels dimmed right now: laughter comes only rarely and feels forced, activities you once anticipated now seem like burdens, and a steady sadness or dread sits in your chest most days. You described nights of lying awake ruminating, sudden waves of panic, and frequent tearfulness that overflows when the house is finally quiet. At the same time, you're working tirelessly to care for your baby, blaming yourself whenever things feel hard, and courageely letting me know you have no thoughts of self-harm. Your honesty highlights how heavy things feel and how much you want relief so you can enjoy being the mom you hoped to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter only "occasionally," which aligns with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame with detailed examples of guilt over normal infant behavior, indicating this happens 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, unprovoked worries that are hard to shake—matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden waves of dread and physical panic symptoms that occur "sometimes," aligning with "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to accomplish tasks despite constant effort, and being immobilized by the mess—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to distressing thoughts, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-constant sadness, heavy chest on waking, and frequent tearfulness—semantically equivalent to "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent crying 3-4 nights weekly, indicating the experience is "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 on the EPDS places well above the 14-point threshold for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The pattern meets <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, insomnia, and clinically significant distress/impairment nearly every day for more than two weeks. Co-occurring <sym>panic-like episodes</sym> and <sym>free-floating anxiety</sym> also suggest comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. The absence of suicidal ideation is reassuring, yet severity warrants prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary-care physician</med> to discuss results and consider medication and/or therapy
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health therapist</med> for cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy
3. Schedule brief check-ins with a trusted adult who can help with night feeds so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted sleep
4. Practice 5-minute paced breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise
5. Limit information overload: choose one evidence-based parenting source and set a timer for social media
6. Continue open conversations with your partner or support person about how you're feeling each evening
7. Keep the national Postpartum Support International warmline number handy: 1-800-944-4PPD for 24/7 encouragement and local resources
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant age not specified  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: Licensed Mental Health Professional  

I. Patient-reported symptoms (EPDS-10 paraphrase)  
- Anhedonia: marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation; rare laughter  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy” daily sadness; crying ≥3 nights/week  
- Excessive guilt/blames self for infant-related issues  
- Anxiety: near-daily, unprovoked worry, racing heart, intrusive catastrophic thoughts about infant safety  
- Panic-like episodes: sudden dread, chest tightness, resolves without trigger  
- Overwhelm: “treading water,” feels frozen facing routine tasks  
- Sleep disturbance: initial/middle insomnia linked to ruminating self-criticism  
- No self-harm ideation (endorsed item 10 as “never”)  

II. Pattern  
Symptoms cluster in depressive (mood, anhedonia, guilt, tearfulness, sleep) and anxiety domains (free-floating worry, panic episodes); functionally impairing; no safety concerns voiced.  

III. Screening significance  
EPDS total estimated ≈ 17–19 (provisional; formal scoring needed). Meets screening threshold for probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; warrants prompt referral to OB/GYN or psychiatry for comprehensive evaluation and possible treatment.
